faq: Moonplan is available on the App Store for iPhone with iOS 17 or later. The app is free to download; Moonplan Premium is an optional subscription.
Which devices and languages does it support?
Moonplan is designed for iPhone with iOS 17 or later. The app is available in English, German, Japanese, Russian, Spanish, French, Portuguese (Brazil) and Italian, and so is this website.
Do I need an account or GPS access?
No. Choose a city yourself, or keep the default city. Moonplan does not request your device’s location or ask you to create an account.
Does it work without the internet?
Yes, lunar calculations, the calendar and the planner run on your device. Looking up a new city requires an internet connection to Apple’s geocoding service.
What are the planning suggestions based on?

They use traditional interpretations of lunar phases and other calendar factors. These cultural traditions are not scientifically established effects, professional advice or promises about an outcome.
Can I use the Japanese calendar?
Yes. The optional Japanese calendar includes old calendar dates, rokuyō and Japanese public holidays. It is enabled automatically when you choose Japanese in the app.
Does Moonplan collect my activity searches?
Planner searches are processed on your device and are not sent to us. City searches are different: the text you enter is sent to Apple so it can find that city.
Email admin@aurelialabs.io. Include your iOS version, the app version and a short description of what happened. Please leave out sensitive personal information.

sections.title: What illumination means
sections.text: Illumination is the share of the visible lunar disc that the Sun lights, from 0% at new Moon to 100% at full Moon. It follows the phase angle, the angle Sun–Moon–Earth: the smaller it is, the more of the disc is lit. Illumination does not grow evenly from day to day: it changes fastest near the quarters and slowest near new and full Moon.

sections.title: The age of the Moon
sections.text: The age is the time since the last new Moon, in days. The interval between two new Moons, the synodic month, averages about 29.5 days, but each one is a little longer or shorter because the Moon’s speed along its orbit varies.

sections.title: Distance and angular diameter
sections.text: The distance is measured from the centre of the Earth to the centre of the Moon. Because the orbit is an ellipse, it varies between roughly 356,000 and 407,000 km. The angular diameter is how large the disc looks in the sky, in arcminutes (′): about 29′ when the Moon is farthest and about 34′ when it is nearest.

sections.title: Libration
sections.text: The Moon always shows us nearly the same face, but it seems to rock slightly. Libration in longitude shifts the view east or west, libration in latitude north or south, by up to a few degrees. Thanks to it we can see a little more than half of the lunar surface over time. The sign shows the direction of the shift.

sections.title: Perigee and apogee
sections.text: Perigee is the point of the Moon’s orbit closest to the Earth, apogee the farthest. They come about once a month, roughly two weeks apart. A full or new Moon near perigee is what is popularly called a supermoon.

sections.title: Lunar eclipses
sections.text: A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon passes through the Earth’s shadow. In a total eclipse the whole disc enters the dark core of the shadow, in a partial one only a part does, and in a penumbral one the Moon only dims slightly in the outer shadow. An eclipse is visible wherever the Moon is above the horizon at that moment.

how: The values come from the Astronomy Engine library (MIT license), which runs in your browser. Positions of the Sun and the Moon are calculated for the exact moment on your device’s clock, and times are shown in your device’s time zone with UTC in small print.
The page does not ask for your location and sends nothing anywhere. Moonrise and moonset are not shown here, because they depend on the place; the Moonplan app shows them for the city you choose.

The picture of the Moon is one of 72 pre-rendered frames, one per 5° of the Sun–Moon elongation, built from NASA’s LRO mosaics. The frame closest to the current phase is chosen and rotated to match the orientation of the lit limb in the sky.
